title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 16: Information Technology Foundation v. Comelec: Flawed Contract for Election Automation
keywords: the end never justifies the means
primary_topics: Chapter 16 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's account of Information Technology Foundation v. Comelec, the case in which the Supreme Court voided the Comelec contract for the automated counting and canvassing of the 2004 votes, a Decision he wrote after his Dissenting Opinion became the majority's ponencia.

His narration of how Comelec gravely abused its discretion: awarding a billion-peso contract to a 'consortium' whose existence and eligibility were never documented, then executing the contract with MPEI alone, in violation of its own bidding rules and the Government Procurement Act.

His account of the technical failures Comelec waived away -- counting machines that missed the 99.9995 percent accuracy rating, could not detect and block previously downloaded results, and lacked an incorporated audit trail -- and of the admission that the software evaluated was only a demo version.

His Epilogue and the Court's disposition: the Resolution and Contract declared void, the payments ordered recovered, the Ombudsman directed to determine criminal liability, and the Motion for Reconsideration denied with finality.
sub_topics: He opens with the decade of failed attempts to automate Philippine elections and a counting system unchanged in a hundred years -- still super-slow and fraud-prone -- and the nation's expectation that the May 10, 2004 presidential elections would be fully automated.

He sets out Comelec's three-phase modernization -- voter list cleanup, automated counting and canvassing, and electronic transmission -- and notes that the first contract fell in Comelec v. Quijano-Padilla and Photokina and the third in Brilliantes v. Comelec.

He discloses the case's internal history: it had been raffled to Justice Tinga, but during the deliberations from December 2003 the majority voted to uphold CJP's Dissenting Opinion, which became the new ponencia.

The facts: RA 8436 of December 22, 1997 authorizing an automated election system; Comelec Resolution 02-0170 adopting the three phases; the January 28, 2003 Invitation to Apply for Eligibility and to Bid; Resolution 5929's eligibility criteria including the twenty-million-voter track record, the 10 percent equity requirement and the 20 percent performance bond.

The bidding: the two-envelope, two-stage system; 57 bidders reduced to Mega Pacific Consortium and Total Information Management Corporation; the DOST technical evaluation that gave both failed marks; and Resolution 6074 of April 15, 2003 awarding the project to MPC anyway.

Locus standi: because the nation's political and economic future hung on the 2004 elections, the subject matter was of paramount public interest and transcendental importance, justifying relaxation of the rule on standing.

Prematurity: the Court held that Comelec en banc, by awarding the project on April 15 before the BAC issued its report on April 21, made it legally impossible for petitioners to use the protest mechanism of RA 9184 -- and in any case the May 29, 2003 letter to Chairman Abalos was a sufficient written protest.

The first ground of grave abuse -- identity and eligibility: no joint venture, consortium or similar instrument was ever submitted, so Comelec had no basis to conclude that a consortium existed, was eligible, could deliver, or that its members were jointly and severally liable.

What surfaced only after the bidding: four separate bilateral agreements instead of one multilateral pact -- MOAs with SK C&C and WeSolv limiting liability to each firm's own area of work, and Teaming Agreements making Election.com and ePLDT mere subcontractors not solidarily liable to Comelec.

The contract itself: 'The Automated Counting and Canvassing Project Contract' was executed between Comelec and MPEI, signed by Willy U. Yu as president of MPEI, with no mention of any consortium, joint venture or joint and several liability -- measured against the definition of joint venture in Kilosbayan v. Guingona.

The second ground -- technical failure: both bidders missed the mandatory 99.9995 percent accuracy rating, and the Court condemned the practice of setting unrealistic specifications only to water them down after the award as a sure indication of fraud that discourages bona fide bidders.

Further technical deficiencies: the machines could not detect previously downloaded precinct, city, municipal and provincial results and prevent their re-entry, opening the way to massive fraud by a few keystrokes; and the audit trail, mandatory under Section 7 of RA 8436, was not yet incorporated into MPC's machines.

The software admission: Commissioner Borra conceded at the Oral Argument that the software then in use was merely the demo version, with the final one still being developed, leaving the Court with the impression that Comelec was keeping its fingers crossed and hoping the final product would work.

Remedial measures and further flaws: 100 percent testing could not cure the grave abuse already committed; the December 15, 2003 MIRDC-DOST letter that Comelec invoked in fact reported hardware testing, not software reprogramming; and permitting the winning bidder to change the software amounted to a substantive amendment without public bidding.

The Epilogue: the Court at the crossroads of the nation's history; Comelec's failure to measure up to its historic task; the finding that it had shoddily accepted hardware and software that admittedly failed legally mandated requirements; the demand that public funds be recovered; and the closing maxims that the end never justifies the means and that penumbral contracting will not produce enlightened results.

The disposition and the Separate Opinions: Resolution 6074 and the MPEI Contract declared null and void, with referrals to the Ombudsman and the Solicitor General; concurrences by Justices Santiago (eligibility, exhaustion, and the midstream change of the accuracy criterion) and Gutierrez (MPEI nonexistent at the time of the Invitation, and mandatory requirements that cannot be waived).

The dissents: Chief Justice Davide on the destabilizing effect of voiding a partly performed contract with no time to re-bid and no suggestion of graft; Justice Vitug on the enormity of the factual disputes making certiorari inapt; and Justice Tinga's extended dissent on the writs invoked, exhaustion, the notarized consortium agreements, solidary liability, collective qualification and the DOST findings -- a 9-5 result with one vacancy.

The Motion for Reconsideration: the same issues re-raised and rejected; the clarification that no criminal prejudgment had been made; the distinction from the Amari and Piatco cases, which were commercial and involved no irregular disbursement, whereas here nearly P850 million of the P1.3 billion had already been irregularly paid; and the denial with finality.

stances.claim: Comelec gravely abused its discretion when it awarded the automation contract to a purported consortium whose existence, composition and joint and several liability were never established by any document submitted during the bidding.
stances.rhetorical_move: evidentiary absence argument: he catalogues what was not in the Eligibility Envelope and what the four belated bilateral agreements actually said, so that the award appears to rest on nothing

stances.claim: Setting very high or unrealistic specifications and then watering them down after the award destroys the essence of public bidding and is a sure indication of fraud designed to eliminate fair competition; if no bidder met the mandatory standards, a failed bidding should have been declared.
stances.rhetorical_move: purpose-of-the-rule reasoning: he returns to why bidding exists -- fair competition and a precise comparison of bids -- and measures Comelec's conduct against that purpose

stances.claim: Awarding a contract on the strength of a demo 'base' software, with the election-day program still to be developed, and then allowing it to be changed afterwards, was a substantive amendment of the bidded subject without public bidding.
stances.rhetorical_move: use of the respondent's own admissions: Borra's concession and Comelec's December 29, 2003 submission are quoted back as the proof of the defect

stances.claim: The void Resolution and Contract required not only nullification but recovery of the public funds already disbursed and referral to the Ombudsman, because for the Court to cop out and close its eyes would be to abandon its constitutional duty of safeguarding public interest.
stances.rhetorical_move: duty-to-act peroration in the Epilogue, framed as a choice between convenience and constitutional obligation

stances.claim: The dissenters argued that the Petition was premature for failure to exhaust the RA 9184 protest remedies, that the notarized consortium agreements predated the bidding deadline, and that the tested machines had in fact satisfied the mandatory AES features.
stances.rhetorical_move: full-length restatement of the opposing case, set out in the dissenters' own sequence of arguments

notable_anecdotes: The dissent that became the ponencia: he discloses that the case had been raffled to Justice Tinga, but that during deliberations beginning in December 2003 the majority voted to uphold his own Dissenting Opinion, which then became the Decision.
Rewinding the clock: he interrupts his own narration -- 'But that is racing ahead too soon' -- to go back and lay out the facts from the beginning.

The impossible remedy: he notes bluntly that Comelec en banc awarded the project on April 15, six days before the BAC issued its report, making it legally impossible for petitioners to appeal the recommendation, and answers the respondents' Latin with their own, Nemo tenetur ad impossibilia.

The commissioner's admission: Commissioner Borra conceded during the Oral Argument that the software in use was merely the demo version, the final one still under development, leaving the Court with the impression that Comelec was keeping its fingers crossed.

The single multilateral agreement that was not: Commissioner Tuason claimed in open court that one agreement bound all five consortium members, but four separate bilateral agreements turned up instead, furnished only after the bidding had ended.

The DOST letter read closely: he quotes the brief December 15, 2003 MIRDC-DOST letter reporting that 1,991 machines had been tested and 18 had failed, and shows that it said nothing at all about the software Comelec claimed it had validated.

The P850 million already paid: in denying reconsideration the Court observed that the government had earmarked P1.3 billion and Comelec had already irregularly paid nearly P850 million, and that the commissioners' outbursts showed they had not realized the gravity of their misdeeds.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' is CJP's account of Information Technology Foundation v. Comelec, in which the Supreme Court voided the contract for automating the counting and canvassing of the 2004 votes. He began with the century-old Philippine counting system, still super-slow and fraud-prone, and with Comelec's three-phase modernization, noting that the first phase contract had already fallen in Comelec v. Quijano-Padilla and Photokina and the third in Brilliantes v. Comelec. He disclosed that the case had been raffled to Justice Tinga but that during deliberations from December 2003 the majority adopted his own dissent as the ponencia. Reviewing the facts -- RA 8436, Comelec's Resolutions, the two-envelope bidding, the fifty-seven bidders narrowed to Mega Pacific Consortium and TIMC, the DOST evaluation giving both failed marks, and the April 15, 2003 award by Resolution 6074 -- he upheld the petitioners' standing because the nation's future hung on the elections, and rejected the claim of prematurity because Comelec en banc had awarded the project six days before the BAC reported, making the statutory protest impossible. On the merits he found grave abuse of discretion on two grounds. First, no consortium agreement was ever submitted, so Comelec had no basis to find MPC existent, eligible, capable or solidarily liable; four bilateral agreements surfaced only after the bidding, limiting each firm's liability, and the Contract itself was signed with MPEI alone, with no mention of any consortium. Second, the counting machines failed the mandatory 99.9995 percent accuracy rating, could not block previously downloaded results -- opening the prospect of massive fraud by a few keystrokes -- and lacked the audit trail required by Section 7 of RA 8436, while Commissioner Borra admitted that the software evaluated was only a demo, leaving Comelec, in the Court's words, keeping its fingers crossed. Post-award testing could not cure the abuse, and allowing the software to be changed was a substantive amendment without bidding. His Epilogue declared that Comelec had failed to measure up to its historic task, ordered the recovery of public funds and referral to the Ombudsman, and closed that the end never justifies the means and that penumbral contracting will not produce enlightened results. He then summarized the concurrences of Justices Santiago and Gutierrez and the dissents of Chief Justice Davide, Justice Vitug and Justice Tinga, a 9-5 result, and the denial with finality of the Motion for Reconsideration.
